# Shear-warp
Also called: Shear-warp factorization

## Overview
The Shear-warp family comprises object-order volume rendering algorithms that accelerate rendering by factorizing the 3D viewing transformation into a 3D shear and a 2D warp [S3, S4, S7, unofficial]. It solves the problem of efficient rendering from arbitrary viewing angles by transforming the volume into a "sheared object space" where viewing rays are parallel to a coordinate axis, allowing for efficient slice-by-slice compositing [S12]. Unlike general ray-casting methods that perform trilinear interpolation per pixel, Shear-warp substitutes this with fixed bilinear interpolation weights computed once per frame, exploiting spatial coherence and memory alignment [S3, S9, unofficial]. It is distinct from pure feed-backward (ray-casting) methods, which cast rays into the data set, and pure feed-forward (element-tossing) methods, which map data elements directly to the image plane [S1, unofficial].

## Shared principles
The Shear-warp family shares the core mechanism of transforming volume data via affine operations to achieve pixel alignment before compositing [S1, unofficial]. This process generally involves two main phases: warping and compositing [S1, unofficial].

1.  **Factorization:** The viewing transformation matrix $M_{view}$ is decomposed into a permutation matrix $P$, a shear matrix $S$, and a 2D warp matrix $M_{warp2D}$ [S2, S4, S7, unofficial]:
    $$ M_{view} = M_{warp2D} \cdot S \cdot P $$
    The permutation $P$ aligns the principal viewing axis with a volume axis (typically Z) to maximize the number of slices perpendicular to the view [S2, unofficial][S12]. The shear $S$ transforms the volume such that viewing rays become parallel to this axis, making them perpendicular to the volume slices [S2, S7, unofficial].

2.  **Shear and Resampling:** Volume slices (perpendicular to the principal axis) are transformed into an intermediate 2D image space [S2, unofficial][S12].
    *   **Shear Coefficients:** For parallel projection, shear coefficients $s_x, s_y$ are calculated from the view direction $v_o = [v_{o,x}, v_{o,y}, v_{o,z}]^T$ in the permuted space:
        $$ s_x = -\frac{v_{o,x}}{v_{o,z}}, \quad s_y = -\frac{v_{o,y}}{v_{o,z}} $$
    *   **Matrix:** The shear matrix for parallel projection is:
        $$ S = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & s_x & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & s_y & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} $$
    *   **Interpolation:** Resampling uses bilinear interpolation within the traversed volume slices [S2, S7, unofficial]. Because the shear ensures sampling rays are perpendicular to the slices, fixed interpolation weights can be computed once per frame [S3, S9, unofficial].
    *   **Optimization:** Run-Length Encoded (RLE) structures are used to skip transparent voxel runs [S2, S3, S4, unofficial]. The intermediate image often stores opaque-pixel offsets to skip occluded pixels, enabling early ray termination [S2, unofficial][S11, abstract only, unofficial].

3.  **Compositing:** The sheared slices are composited in front-to-back order into the intermediate image using the Porter-Duff "over" operator [S2, unofficial][S12]:
    $$ C_{new} = C_{slice} \cdot \alpha_{slice} + C_{accum} \cdot (1 - \alpha_{slice}) $$
    $$ \alpha_{new} = \alpha_{slice} + \alpha_{accum} \cdot (1 - \alpha_{slice}) $$
    Early ray termination stops processing further slices for a pixel if accumulated opacity $\alpha_{accum}$ exceeds a threshold (e.g., 0.95) [S2, unofficial][S11, abstract only, unofficial].

4.  **Warp:** The intermediate image is transformed to the final image space using the 2D warp matrix $M_{warp2D}$ [S2, unofficial][S12]:
    $$ M_{warp2D} = M_{view} \cdot S^{-1} \cdot P^{-1} $$
    (Note: Some sources define $M_{warp2D} = M_{view} \cdot M_{shear}^{-1}$ assuming $P$ is handled in the permutation step [S7, S21, unofficial].) This step corrects the distortion introduced by the shear and applies the correct perspective/parallel projection [S22, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [VolumePro Ray-Casting with Slice-by-Slice Processing](1865-volumepro-ray-casting-with-slice-by-slice-processing.md)
VolumePro is a specialized hardware architecture that implements object-space ray-casting with parallel slice-by-slice processing to achieve real-time frame rates on PC-class computers. It differs from texture-mapping approaches by supporting gradient estimation and per-sample Phong illumination in real-time, and from pre-processing approaches by allowing immediate visual feedback during parameter changes without lengthy recomputation. It builds on the Shear-warp method [24-shear-warp.md] by casting rays from the base plane (the volume face most parallel to the viewing plane) into the dataset, projecting the resulting base plane image onto the final image plane via a 3D transformation and 2D warping.

### [Affine-Transformations Method](2038-affine-transformations-method.md)
The Affine-Transformations Method is a hybrid volume rendering technique that uses affine transformations to warp volume slices or the entire volume into the image plane so that data samples become pixel-aligned, after which the transformed data is composited to calculate visibility. It is distinct from pure feed-backward (ray-casting) methods, which cast rays into the data set, and pure feed-forward (element-tossing) methods, which map data elements directly to the image plane. By aligning samples with pixels before compositing, it bridges the gap between these two extremes, leveraging the efficiency of feed-forward warping while maintaining the visibility handling of feed-backward approaches.

### [Shear-Warp Algorithm](4304-shear-warp-algorithm.md)
The Shear-Warp Algorithm is a fast, software-based volume rendering technique that reduces the number of resampling passes from three to two by factorizing the viewing transformation matrix into a 3D shear and a 2D warp. It solves the problem of efficient rendering from arbitrary viewing angles by transforming the volume data into a "sheared object space" where viewing rays are parallel to a coordinate axis, allowing for efficient slice-by-slice compositing. Unlike general ray-casting methods that perform trilinear interpolation per pixel, Shear-Warp substitutes this with fixed bilinear interpolation weights computed once per frame, exploiting spatial coherence and memory alignment. It is distinct from GPU-based ray marching by relying on CPU-driven affine transformations and intermediate image buffers, though it shares the slice-based processing logic with [Affine-Transformations Method](2038-affine-transformations-method.md).

### [Parallel Projection Rendering](5556-parallel-projection-rendering.md)
Parallel Projection Rendering is an object-order volume rendering algorithm optimized for parallel viewing transformations, utilizing run-length encoded (RLE) data structures to exploit spatial coherence in both the volume and the intermediate image. It builds on the Shear-warp factorization [Parent](24-shear-warp.md) but specifically targets parallel projections where all voxel slices share a uniform scale factor, allowing a one-to-one mapping between sheared voxel scanlines and intermediate image pixels. Unlike general shear-warp implementations that may require multiple resampling passes, this method minimizes resampling to two steps (shear and final 2D warp) and achieves significant performance gains by skipping transparent voxels and occluded pixels via RLE traversal.

### [Perspective Projection Rendering](5558-perspective-projection-rendering.md)
Perspective Projection Rendering extends the Shear-warp algorithm to support perspective viewing transformations by scaling each volume slice in addition to shearing it. It solves the problem of rendering 3D volumes with perspective projection, which introduces foreshortening that standard parallel projection shear-warp methods cannot handle. Unlike the [Parallel Projection Rendering](5556-parallel-projection-rendering.md) variant, it accounts for depth-dependent scaling, ensuring that farther slices are rendered smaller to match perspective geometry.

### [Hybrid Shear-Warp and Polygon Rendering](5876-hybrid-shear-warp-and-polygon-rendering.md)
This method extends the Shear-warp algorithm to correctly intermix polygonal geometry with volume rendering in a single pass. It solves the problem of visual artifacts when opaque polygons occlude volume data or are occluded by it, ensuring correct concurrent display. Unlike pure volume renderers, it integrates a polygon rendering stage and uses an inversely warped Z-buffer to limit viewing rays during compositing.

### [Perspective Shear-Warp](6047-perspective-shear-warp.md)
Perspective Shear-Warp is a volume rendering technique that extends the parallel Shear-warp method to support perspective projections by applying a distance-dependent scale factor during the shear phase. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering large 3D datasets with perspective cameras by reducing the 3D ray-casting problem to a series of 2D texture lookups and compositing operations, avoiding the need to calculate individual viewing ray trajectories. Unlike parallel Shear-warp, which assumes parallel viewing rays, this method accounts for ray divergence, making it suitable for close-up views or views from within the volume, though it incurs higher computational cost due to additional resampling.

### [VolumePro 500 Implementation](8161-volumepro-500-implementation.md)
The VolumePro 500 is a hardware-accelerated volume rendering system based on the Cube-4 architecture that implements the Shear-warp algorithm. It distinguishes itself from software implementations by using specialized memory address arithmetic called 3D skewing to efficiently read axis-aligned voxel slices while storing only one copy of the volume data. Unlike general-purpose GPU ray-casting, it processes data in a brute-force manner where performance is independent of classification complexity or data sparsity, relying on fixed-function hardware for interpolation, gradient estimation, and shading.

### Back-to-front polygon rendering with display lists
Renders parallel polygons from back to front to satisfy linear alpha blending requirements for compositing [S8, unofficial]. The method defines six display lists (two directions along each of three axes). The renderer determines the largest absolute component of the view vector (x, y, or z) and its sign, then executes the corresponding display list [S8, unofficial]. A pitfall is that polygons are never viewed edge-on, limiting oblique viewing angles [S8, unofficial].

### Shear-Warp Factorization Rendered Examples Pipeline
The pipeline components include a gradient processor, matrix multiplication processor, shader, and classifier [S9, unofficial]. The process applies a rotation transformation matrix $M_{rot}$ with rotation angle $\alpha$ to the volume data [S9, unofficial]. It applies classification transfer functions to make soft tissues completely transparent, leaving only bone surfaces visible [S9, unofficial]. Finally, it applies a Phong fast lighting model to shade the image [S9, unofficial].

### Coordinate System Conventions
A set of six distinct coordinate systems is used to track transformations in the shear-warp algorithm, each identified by a unique single character [S10, unofficial]. Transition matrices between coordinate systems are named using the source and destination identifiers, e.g., $M_{ow}$ for object-to-world, and $M_{wo}$ for world-to-object [S10, unofficial]. The systems are: 'o' (object space, actual volume data coordinates), 's' (standard object space, after permutation), 'd' (deformed space, 3D coordinates after shear), 'i' (intermediate image space, 2D coordinates within intermediate image), 'w' (world coordinate space), and 'v' (viewport space, 2D output window coordinates) [S10, unofficial].

### Parallel Shear-Warp on Shared Memory
A parallel volume rendering algorithm for shared-memory multiprocessors that minimizes computation, synchronization, and data communication time [S10, unofficial]. The algorithm is based on the shear-warp serial volume rendering algorithm to minimize computation time [S10, unofficial]. It minimizes synchronization time by using dynamic load balancing and a task partition that minimizes synchronization events [S10, unofficial]. It is implemented for shared-memory multiprocessors to leverage hardware support for low-latency fine-grain communication and hardware caching to hide latency [S10, unofficial]. A pitfall is that cache locality requirements impose a limit on parallelism; shared-memory machines with hundreds of processors are only useful for rendering very large data sets [S10, unofficial].

### Parallel Projection Rendering 3
This variant uses bilinear interpolation and backward projection convolution [S4, unofficial]. It traverses 2 voxel scanlines simultaneously to produce one intermediate image scanline, which lies between the two voxel scanlines [S4, unofficial]. It uses a lookup table for shading and another lookup table to correct voxel opacity for view angle, accounting for apparent slice thickness dependence on angle [S4, unofficial]. After compositing, it warps the 2D intermediate image to the final image using a general purpose affine image warper with bilinear filter [S4, unofficial]. The run length encoded data structure is created on the fly, but is nearly view-independent, with 3 encodings created for each principal view direction [S4, unofficial]. A pitfall is that transparent voxels are not stored, so the size is usually tractable [S4, unofficial].

### Gaussian Volumetric Representation for Shear-Warp Visualization
A Gaussian-based volumetric representation proposed to address the high computational cost of large volumetric datasets while preserving anatomical fidelity and maintaining high rendering speeds in Shear-Warp visualization [S11, abstract only, unofficial].

### Warping Fields
A technique using a template RGB$\alpha$ volume $T(x)$ and a warp volume $W^{-1}(x)$ to alter effective voxel resolution and model motion, where $W^{-1}$ maps output positions to template sample locations [S12]. The final volume value is computed by first evaluating the value of the inverse warp $W^{-1}(x)$, then sampling the template volume $T$ at the resulting warped point [S12]. A pitfall is that forward warps cannot represent resolution-increasing transformations without additional memory; inverse warps map small output areas to larger template areas, allowing higher resolution details while remaining well-defined everywhere for usable gradients [S12].

## Background
The Shear-warp algorithm was designed by Lacroute et al. in 1994 [S2, S7, unofficial]. It was recognized as the fastest software render algorithm at the time [S2, unofficial]. The basic idea is to factorize the projection matrix into a 3D shear and 2D warp [S1, unofficial]. Using the shearing, the data set is transformed into sheared object space where all viewing rays are parallel to one coordinate axis [S1, unofficial]. The volume is considered as a stack of 2D slices, which are composited into an intermediate image, which is then warped to the image plane [S1, S3, unofficial].

The algorithm was implemented in specialized hardware, VolumePro, which was the first single-chip hardware compatible with consumer PCs for real-time volume rendering [S2, unofficial]. VolumePro was based on the Cube-4 framework and specialized for the Shear-warp algorithm [S2, unofficial]. It used trilinear interpolation instead of linear interpolation for better image quality and incorporated features like super-sampling and cropping [S2, unofficial].

The algorithm has been adapted for GPU acceleration, with implementations claiming to be the first on the GPU, providing real-time frame rates and outperforming CPU-based implementations [S7, unofficial]. GPU-based implementations store volume data in 3D textures and render slices as textured quadrilaterals, using vertex shaders for shearing and fragment shaders for shading and compositing [S7, unofficial].
